title: Izhikevich Model
intro: The Izhikevich model adds a slow recovery variable to a quadratic integrate-and-fire neuron. Four parameters (a, b, c, d) switch it between regular spiking, bursting, chattering, fast-spiking and low-threshold-spiking behaviour at a cost close to LIF, which makes it a popular choice for heterogeneous cortical columns.

blocks.text: Intuition: LIF plus a slow brake

A leaky integrate-and-fire neuron has a single state variable, so it can only do one thing: fire regularly at a rate set by its input. Real cortical neurons have a repertoire. Regular-spiking pyramidal cells fire a few fast spikes and then slow down (adaptation); intrinsically bursting cells start with a burst; chattering cells fire repetitive high-frequency bursts at gamma-range rates; fast-spiking interneurons fire at hundreds of hertz with almost no adaptation. Most of this variety comes from slow currents that build up during firing and push the membrane back down.

Eugene Izhikevich (2003) captured this with two variables. The fast variable v is the membrane potential, and its quadratic term makes the upswing of the spike self-accelerating (unlike LIF, there is a genuine spike-initiation dynamic). The slow variable u is a recovery variable that lumps together potassium activation and sodium inactivation: it is pulled towards b·v at rate a, and kicked up by d after every spike. Four numbers (a, b, c, d) select the firing type. The result is roughly as cheap as LIF but reproduces most cortical firing patterns.

blocks.source:
dv/dt = 0.04·v² + 5·v + 140 − u + I
du/dt = a · (b·v − u)

if v ≥ 30 mV:   v ← c,   u ← u + d

v in mV, t in ms; I is a dimensionless input (in effect mV/ms, membrane capacitance and resistance absorbed)
a  time scale of u (small a = slow recovery)        typical 0.02
b  sensitivity of u to sub-threshold v              typical 0.2
c  after-spike reset of v (mV)                      typical −65
d  after-spike increment of u                       typical 2–8

blocks.text: Note what the 30 mV value is: it is the spike peak at which the model is cut off and reset, not a threshold. The effective threshold is emergent: with the regular-spiking parameters and no input, the model has a stable resting point at −70 mV and an unstable threshold point at about −50 mV, and both shift as u changes (with b = 0.25 the rest is nearer −64 mV). Because the constant input I has no explicit units, the canonical numbers only make sense together with the 1 ms network time step and the input scaling of the original code; for the regular-spiking parameters the two fixed points merge, and tonic firing starts, at a constant I of about 4.
These are the (a, b, c, d) values from Figure 2 of the 2003 paper. The cortical excitatory classes differ mainly in the reset c and the adaptation step d; the inhibitory classes mainly in a and b.

blocks.text: Reading the table: a larger d means a bigger after-spike kick to u, hence stronger spike-frequency adaptation (RS). A higher reset c leaves v close to the spike-initiation region, so the next spike follows quickly and the cell bursts (IB, CH). A larger a makes u recover quickly, so FS cells can fire at high, nearly constant rates. A larger b couples u more strongly to sub-threshold v, which gives LTS cells their low threshold and rebound behaviour. The mapping of firing types to cell classes in the right-hand column is the conventional one, but it is a simplification: real classes are defined by morphology, molecular markers and connectivity as well as firing (see "Cell Types" in section 1).

The original MATLAB network in the 2003 paper uses a 1 ms time step but updates v in two half-steps of 0.5 ms each, 'for numerical stability', and updates u once. Because the quadratic term makes v blow up quickly near the peak, a plain 1 ms Euler step on v can overshoot badly; the two half-steps are a cheap fix. The snippet below follows that scheme, including the random heterogeneity trick from the paper: excitatory cells interpolate between RS (r = 0) and CH (r = 1) via r², inhibitory cells between FS and LTS.

blocks.source:
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

Ne, Ni = 800, 200
re, ri = rng.random(Ne), rng.random(Ni)
a = np.r_[0.02 * np.ones(Ne), 0.02 + 0.08 * ri]
b = np.r_[0.20 * np.ones(Ne), 0.25 - 0.05 * ri]
c = np.r_[-65 + 15 * re**2,   -65 * np.ones(Ni)]
d = np.r_[8 - 6 * re**2,      2 * np.ones(Ni)]
S = np.c_[0.5 * rng.random((Ne + Ni, Ne)), -rng.random((Ne + Ni, Ni))]  # S[post, pre]

v = -65.0 * np.ones(Ne + Ni)
u = b * v
firings = []
for t in range(1000):                                   # 1000 steps of 1 ms
    I = np.r_[5 * rng.standard_normal(Ne), 2 * rng.standard_normal(Ni)]  # noisy thalamic input
    fired = np.flatnonzero(v >= 30)
    firings += [(t, i) for i in fired]
    v[fired] = c[fired]
    u[fired] += d[fired]
    I += S[:, fired].sum(axis=1)                        # instantaneous synapses, no delay
    v += 0.5 * (0.04 * v**2 + 5 * v + 140 - u + I)      # two 0.5 ms half-steps for v
    v += 0.5 * (0.04 * v**2 + 5 * v + 140 - u + I)
    u += a * (b * v - u)

blocks.text: Run it and plot the firings as a raster: you should see irregular firing punctuated by population rhythms in the alpha and gamma ranges, which was the point of the original demonstration. For serious work, use a smaller step (0.1–0.25 ms) or an established simulator. Brian2 accepts the equations directly as a model string with threshold 'v >= 30*mV' and reset 'v = c; u += d' (you will need to attach units to the coefficients); NEST provides an izhikevich model; and many neuromorphic toolchains support it as well.

In a companion paper, Izhikevich (2004) compared spiking models by the number of biologically observed firing features they can reproduce and by their cost per 1 ms of simulation. His estimates were roughly 5 floating-point operations for LIF, 13 for his model, and about 1200 for Hodgkin–Huxley. Treat these as order-of-magnitude figures (they depend on the integration scheme), but the conclusion stands: the Izhikevich model gives you most of the firing-pattern variety of a conductance model at a cost close to LIF. In practice, for a column of a few thousand to a hundred thousand neurons the neuron update is rarely the bottleneck; synaptic event processing is.
When to use it in a column model

items: Use Izhikevich neurons when the dynamics you study depend on firing type: bursting layer-5 output cells, adapting regular-spiking excitatory cells versus non-adapting FS interneurons, rebound in thalamic cells, or oscillations that depend on these differences.

Use LIF (possibly with adaptation) when the question is about connectivity, learning rules or representations (SDRs, k-WTA, STDP) rather than single-cell dynamics. LIF has interpretable parameters (τm, θ, R) and an analytic f–I curve; the Izhikevich parameters are phenomenological.

A reasonable default for a layered column: RS for excitatory cells in layers 2/3, 4 and 6, a mix of RS and IB for layer 5, FS for parvalbumin-like interneurons, LTS for somatostatin-like interneurons. Document this as a modelling choice, not a biological fact.

If you later want to fit real recordings, the AdEx model (Brette & Gerstner 2005) or Izhikevich's later form C·dv/dt = k(v − v_r)(v − v_t) − u + I (Izhikevich 2007) have parameters in physical units, which makes fitting easier.

Integration error: the quadratic term is stiff near spike onset. A 1 ms Euler step on v without the half-step trick produces wrong spike times and can produce NaNs. If you change dt, re-check the f–I curve.
Units: I is not in nA. Do not plug synaptic currents calibrated for a LIF neuron with R = 10 MΩ into the Izhikevich equation unchanged; rescale until single-cell f–I curves look right.
The spike peak is clipped: v reaching 30 mV is a cutoff, not a physiological peak. If you record v and compute averages (e.g. LFP proxies), the clipped spike shapes will bias them.
Grid-locked spikes: with a 1 ms step, spikes land on a 1 ms grid. STDP windows of 10–20 ms tolerate that, but sub-millisecond coincidence detection does not.

The original network uses instantaneous synapses (input added in the same step) and dense random connectivity; that is a dynamics demo, not a cortical column. Add delays, sparse connectivity and synaptic kinetics before drawing conclusions (see "Synapse Models").
